verdicts.evidence: Reuters: French officials 'on Monday accused Iran's Revolutionary Guards of responsibility' for the October attacks. NPR: ANSSI said Iranian military hackers 'took over refrigeration controllers at around 700 different retail sites in France'. Barrot confirmed IRGC responsibility (The Record). Tag ALLEGED is right.
NPR: on Tuesday Iran's Foreign Ministry rejected 'baseless and malicious allegations'.

True as to governments: The Record (Nov. 9) says the ANSSI report 'doesn't address' the November wave; Reuters gives no attribution for it. But a public claim of responsibility exists and the page omits it: Help Net Security (Nov. 9) refers to 'NoName057(16) or Z-Pentest, the groups that claimed the supermarket attacks' and says investigators have not confirmed the claims; SentinelOne (Nov. 3-4) describes the NoName057(16) video naming Danfoss and Dixell XWEB gear, 'not independently verified'; TechTimes (Nov. 10) says the two groups claimed the November wave. Flat 'unattributed' drops that.
verdicts.fix: No government has attributed the November wave, the blood service attack or the U.S. commissary failures. Pro-Russian groups NoName057(16) and Z-Pentest have claimed the supermarket attacks; investigators have not confirmed those claims. U.S. officials, speaking anonymously, suspect Iran-linked hackers in the commissary cases.

verdicts.evidence: Advisory 'US Government Partners Urge Hardening Industrial Refrigeration and Cold Chain Monitoring Systems', 'As of November 5, 2026', authored by CISA, FBI, HHS, USDA and DoT.

The 700 figure is the minister's, not the prosecutor's. AP: Roland Lescure told Parliament 'about 700 of the country's 10,000 supermarkets were affected'; the Paris prosecutor's office said only that its 'cybercrime unit was investigating the large-scale attack' and gave no number (AP, ITV). Reuters Oct. 12: prosecutor described 'several major food retailers', no count. ANSSI (about 700) and Barrot ('more than 700 ... on October 11 and 12') gave figures later. Night of Oct. 11-12 is supported (IT-Connect, TechTimes).
verdicts.fix: ~700 French food retailers hit on the night of Oct. 11 to 12, per the economy minister (to Parliament, Oct. 13) and, later, ANSSI.

verdicts.evidence: Reuters: fridges and freezers 'as high as 50 degrees Celsius' for about six hours at Intermarche stores, 'sparking fires'. AP: '50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit)' per BFM-TV. The Record: at least 15 fires. Note: the six-hour duration rests on Reuters/Intermarche alone; 'at some stores' keeps it in bounds.
The Hacker News: 'Danfoss declared the AK-SM 800 end-of-life in May 2021 and phased out the AK-SC 355 in 2016.'

Nextgov, Oct. 28: 'Several steps still stand between the program and labeled products reaching store shelves'; 'The FCC must finish its technical requirements and testing procedures' before test labs are accredited. The article never says 'zero' in terms; it follows from no lab being accredited. No later report of a certified product found (search, Nov. 10).

Labeled inference. EFS: 'monitoring and alarm systems quickly detected the temperature change' (BleepingComputer); an on-call technician spotted the rise (Le Quotidien du Medecin, IT-Connect). No patch is reported.

Le Quotidien du Medecin, citing Le Canard enchaine: cold rooms 'ont ete programmees pour atteindre 110 C'. IT-Connect: 'Cela ne signifie pas que les poches de plasma ont atteint 110 C'. Newsweek: attackers 'changed the setting to 110 degrees'. Cited FrenchBreaches and U.S. Sun could not be opened; verified on other outlets.
The Hacker News: AK-SM 800A units hit 'were running outdated firmware, according to Danfoss's statement'. Reuters: affected units 'were running outdated firmware'.
The Record: Danfoss's October newsletter said it was enforcing a 'hard End of Service' policy for legacy products. The Hacker News dates the newsletter to October 2025.
The Record, Nov. 2: Danfoss and Copeland both said the affected devices were mainly discontinued products that no longer received security updates.
The Record: Sabcobel knew of about 20 affected units, which 'needed physical modifications and not just a software update'.

The Register, Oct. 13: 'more than 4,500 endpoints were exposed as of Monday, with more than half of those located in France'. Timing is loose: the count is as of Monday Oct. 12, the day after the attack, not 'days after'.
verdicts.fix: Optional tightening, not blocking: 'the day after the attack'.

verdicts.evidence: Claroty: '2765 exposed devices according to Censys'; CVE-2025-41450, -41451, -41452; fixes in 4.2 (for -41450) and R4.3.1. CISA ICSA-25-140-03 (May 20, 2025) covers only CVE-2025-41450 and R4.2; the other two CVEs and R4.3.1 rest on Claroty and Danfoss.
Hackread, Oct. 26: 12,976 exposed observations in 99 countries and territories (Forescout Vedere Labs); Danfoss StoreView 4,697 services. 'Services' is the right unit; they map to 6,017 IP addresses.

The Register, Sept. 2, 2025: ten Frostbyte10 flaws found by Armis in Copeland E2 and E3; E2 end of life in October; Copeland's Josh Weaver: 'about two-thirds of grocery stores in North America use its products'.

Accurate for Oct. 13 but stale, and the product is not named. Reuters Oct. 13: agency said 'the refrigeration systems of Copeland and Dixell were also hacked'; Copeland 'declined to confirm the information'. SecurityWeek Oct. 15: CERT-FR added Copeland XWEB and Dixell XWEB to its alert; Copeland 'first declined to confirm the findings but later acknowledged a vulnerability' and said 'We are currently working with impacted customers'. Newsweek: 'Copeland confirmed a vulnerability in some discontinued controllers'. The compromised line reported is XWEB, not the E2/E3 in the table row this sentence points to.
verdicts.fix: France's cyber agency said Copeland XWEB and Dixell XWEB systems were also compromised in October; Copeland at first declined to confirm, then acknowledged a vulnerability in some discontinued controllers.

verdicts.evidence: 'Direct' was dropped, which reverses the sense. AFP via Boursorama, Oct. 13: the CEO said the group is 'pas clients directs de Danfoss' and 'Nous sommes clients d'acteurs frigoristes qui nous mettent a disposition cette solution'. He is saying the Danfoss system reaches U stores through contractors, not that U does not use it. 80 of about 2,000 stores is supported (AP). The cited Reuters/Star piece does not mention Cooperative U at all.
verdicts.fix: Cooperative U, which had 80 stores hit, says it is not a direct Danfoss customer: it buys from refrigeration contractors that supply the system.

verdicts.evidence: Read the advisory itself: no U.S. incident reported; activity described as 'targeting industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems globally'; refers only to 'malicious cyber actors'. Nextgov: 'The U.S. notice does not name who is responsible'.

Open as of Nov. 10. The Register, Nov. 5: it knows of no documented attacks on refrigeration in U.S. supermarkets. Help Net Security, Nov. 9: no U.S. victims among named countries. Military commissaries are the only U.S. cases, and those are 'suspected'.
Labeled inference describing the page's own scale.

Inference claims more than its facts. The page itself says 'some current AK-SM 800A units were also hit' and that Copeland/Dixell gear was compromised; those are not shown to predate the rules. Only the AK-SC 355 (phased out 2016) clearly predates all of them; the AK-SM 800 was sold until 2021, after California SB 327 took effect (Jan. 1, 2020).
verdicts.fix: Most of the freezer controllers that failed were legacy models sold before most of these rules took effect.

verdicts.evidence: Commission: from 11 September 2026 early warning within 24 hours, notification within 72 hours, final report 'no later than 14 days after a corrective measure is available'. Art. 13(8): 'the support period shall be at least five years' unless expected use is shorter. Main obligations from 11 December 2027 (Jones Day). See flag on the 'NO' cell beside it.
SGS: from 1 August 2025 RED cybersecurity requirements (Art. 3.3 d/e/f) mandatory for 'all radio equipment placed on the market'; EN 18031-1/-2/-3 harmonized standards.
heise: update guarantee of five years 'after the end of sales', in force June 20, 2025.

UK: regime 'came into effect on 29 April 2024'; prohibits universal default passwords; requires published minimum security update period (gov.uk). WATCH half: gov.uk lists no enforcement action; searches on Nov. 10 turned up no OPSS penalty under PSTI. The claim is worded as 'found', which is as far as the record goes. The cited Modern Regulator page could not be opened.

SB 327: 'a reasonable security feature or features'; a preprogrammed password 'unique to each device manufactured' qualifies; operative January 1, 2020; devices 'sold or offered for sale in California'.
Nextgov: 'voluntary program'; FCC 'selected ioXt Alliance as lead administrator in April'.
Same basis as c008: implied by Nextgov (testing requirements and lab accreditation still pending), not stated outright. REPORTED is the right ceiling.
FTC: 'for the next 10 years' Deere must make dealer-equivalent repair resources available to farmers and independent repair providers 'on fair and reasonable terms'. DTN concurs.
DOJ, April 7, 2026: 'court-authorized technical operation'; FBI sent commands to compromised TP-Link routers.

The Register: CERT-FR 'advised disconnecting or restricting network access' and 'recommended a factory reset, security patches, credential rotation'. Alert CERTFR-2026-ALE-012 published Oct. 12 (The Hacker News).

New row; read against the advisory itself. Mitigations: do not expose controllers to the internet; change default passwords; separate OT devices from business networks; 'identify, retire, and replace' devices no longer supported. Dated Nov. 5, 2026. 'Guidance, not a duty' fits: 'provided as is for informational purposes only'.
DTN: compliance reports to the FTC every 60 days, verified by the CEO. FTC release says only 'strict reporting and oversight requirements'.
DTN: Deere must use 'reasonable best efforts' to get approval from a third party whose software is embedded; until then ECU capabilities are not required. Extensions on showing 'good cause'.
Commission: 'As of 11 September 2026, manufacturers are required to report actively exploited vulnerabilities'; early warning within 24 hours; submitted through ENISA's Single Reporting Platform.

The reporting duty does reach them. CRA Art. 69(3): the Article 14 reporting obligations 'apply to all products with digital elements that were placed on the market before 11 December 2027, whether or not they are ever modified' (cyberresilienceact.eu quoting the article); Jones Day: reporting covers products 'already placed on the market before December 11, 2027'. What does not reach installed controllers is the duty to design securely and to support for five years. The untagged sentence above it, 'The rule works at the point of sale', and the table cell 'NO Products placed on the market' carry the same error. 'Enforcement is untested' is fair.
verdicts.fix: Limit: the reporting duty covers products already in the field, but it makes the maker report, not patch; the design and support duties do not reach controllers already on store walls, and enforcement is untested.

verdicts.evidence: heise: five years of updates 'after the end of sales'.
heise: Google 7 years; Samsung 7 for flagships, 6 for A-series; Honor 7 for top models, 'at least 6' for others.
heise: Motorola's lawyers say the regulation 'merely stipulates that updates must be made available free of charge', not 'a guaranteed obligation'.
DOJ: GRU unit 26165 hijacked TP-Link routers; FBI reset DNS settings and blocked the GRU's original access; 'in more than 23 states' (FBI Boston SAC, in the release).
DOJ: steps 'can be reversed by legitimate users at any time through factory resets'; no count of remediated U.S. routers, only 'thousands' compromised worldwide.
Labeled inference. Facts beneath it hold: CERT-FR alert Oct. 12; Reuters: PM Lecornu 'instructed ... ANSSI to investigate'.
Labeled inference. Facts beneath it hold: attribution, summons, warrants and sanctions push on Nov. 9-10, four weeks after Oct. 11-12 (Reuters, Al Jazeera, The Record). None imposes a duty on makers.
Labeled inference; the table's supported rows bear it out.
The Record: Danfoss enforcing 'hard End of Service' for legacy products; the affected devices were mainly discontinued products without security updates.

ADT deal and OpenAI stake are supported (ADT release: '$10.00 per share in cash', '$15.3 billion in enterprise value', Oct. 29; OpenAI, Dec. 1, 2025: 'takes an ownership stake in Thrive Holdings'). The Apple clause is not. TidBITS: 'Apple Retail offers third-party installation from ADT for an additional charge'. It does not say installation happens 'at Apple stores'; the cameras are LG products in the Apple Home Collection, not 'Apple's'; and the line is 'available starting in December 2026', so nothing is being installed yet. One outlet, so FACT is also too strong for that clause.
verdicts.source_read: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001703056/000119312526437123/d572133dex991.htm (ADT release as filed on Form 8-K); https://openai.com/index/thrive-holdings; https://tidbits.com/2026/10/22/apple-home-collection-introduces-new-cameras-doorbell-lock-and-thermostats/
verdicts.fix: Apple says its retail arm will offer ADT installation, for a fee, for the Apple Home Collection, whose LG-made cameras go on sale in December 2026. (REPORTED)

verdicts.evidence: ADT release: go-shop '30 days continuing until 11:59 p.m., New York City time, November 28, 2026' (10-day extension possible for certain parties); 'expected to close in the first quarter of 2027'.

Virginia Code 46.2-507(H)(9): 'an electronic log of the driver's experience' and a system 'capable of electronically delivering information to the Commission within 24 hours'; nothing on confidentiality, access or retention. Matches the home claim in Brief 009 (FACT there). Slate: Carscoops: 'doesn't include an embedded cellular modem'; 'the connection only works when the phone is physically near the EV'.
Still open on Nov. 10. InsideEVs: customer deliveries 'could start as early as December'. Note Carscoops (June) had said 'not due until mid-2027'. Cited Solar Builder page would not load.

gov.uk: regime prohibits universal default passwords, in effect 29 April 2024. No U.S. federal equivalent; California allows a unique preprogrammed password. 'May' keeps the second half within bounds.

The same claim is REPORTED in the hero stat and in the section 04 table (c008, c031), and its only source is one outlet that implies it rather than states it (Nextgov: 'Several steps still stand between the program and labeled products reaching store shelves'). FACT here is a stronger tag than the claim carries at home. The UK and EU halves are fine as FACT.
verdicts.fix: Split the tag: '... In the U.S. no label is required. (FACT) The Cyber Trust Mark had no labeled products as of Oct. 28. (REPORTED)'

verdicts.evidence: DOJ: FBI changes 'can be reversed ... through factory resets with hardware reset buttons'. The advice sentence follows from it.
Labeled inference; rests on supported facts (spoiled food, fires, blood service).
Phones: five years after end of sale since June 20, 2025 (heise). CRA Art. 13(8): support period 'at least five years'; main obligations from 11 December 2027.
Labeled inference; argument for one side, presented as such.
The Record: Sabcobel units 'needed physical modifications and not just a software update'.

The Hacker News: Danfoss's October 2025 newsletter 'said it would end all services for such older products and urged customers to plan replacements'; The Register: Danfoss 'has consistently advocated for keeping systems updated'.
The Hacker News: CERT-FR 'told operators to disconnect the controllers or filter access to them'. SecurityWeek: 'take them off the internet'.
Labeled inference; argument for one side.
Labeled inference; no source and none claimed.

New block. TechTimes and The Record: ANSSI's report names Shahid Kaveh, 'an offensive cyber unit' in the IRGC's Electronic and Cyber Center. NPR: ANSSI cites 'digital infrastructure used by the hackers', a connection to a propaganda outlet and 'traces' of Farsi. ALLEGED is the right tag. Note The Record lists 'Farsi text artefacts, tooling, and infrastructure' and does not tie the propaganda outlet to this unit; NPR and TechTimes do.

Al Jazeera: Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau opened an investigation into Shahid Kaveh; 'The prosecutor's office has requested international arrest warrants be issued for two Shahid Kaveh officials.' REPORTED (one outlet) is right. Other outlets differ on the count: The Record says the investigation covers the unit's head and two deputies and gives no warrant number; TechTimes says warrants for the leader and two deputies.
NPR quotes Ari Ben Am (FDD) and Alex Orleans (Sublime Security): the group 'is repeating a pattern here'. They say it fits the unit's record; neither verified it. 'Plausible' does not exceed that.
NPR: Iran's Foreign Ministry rejected 'baseless and malicious allegations'.

No other government has joined: NPR: Rubio declined to say whether the U.S. shared information; TechTimes: Kallas urged a strong response, 'no specific EU measures'; The Record reports no allied statement and no independent confirmation. Two things the editor should see: (1) the ANSSI report is public (CERTFR-2026-CTI-009, linked by The Record), so 'not the statement itself' is a choice, not a necessity; I could not open it either. (2) TechTimes says Reuters reported Microsoft privately linked Iran to the October sabotage and declined comment; I could not find that in the Reuters copy I read.
Labeled inference; a standard caution, not contradicted by any source read.

True as to governments: The Record (Nov. 9) says the ANSSI report 'doesn't address' the November wave; Reuters gives no attribution for it. But a public claim of responsibility exists and the page omits it: Help Net Security (Nov. 9) refers to 'NoName057(16) or Z-Pentest, the groups that claimed the supermarket attacks' and says investigators have not confirmed the claims; SentinelOne (Nov. 3-4) describes the NoName057(16) video naming Danfoss and Dixell XWEB gear, 'not independently verified'; TechTimes (Nov. 10) says the two groups claimed the November wave. Flat 'unattributed' drops that. The ANSSI report does also allege the same hackers hit small hydroelectric plants, so 'covers France in October' is right.
verdicts.fix: The accusation covers France in October. No government has attributed the November wave, the blood service attack or the U.S. base failures. Pro-Russian groups NoName057(16) and Z-Pentest have claimed the supermarket attacks, unconfirmed; U.S. officials anonymously suspect Iran-linked hackers at the bases.

verdicts.evidence: Labeled inference tying to an in-development piece.

New checkpoint (the whole item, not only its last sentence). Part of it is already answered: France has published. The Record: 'A five-page report from France's Cyber Crisis Coordination Centre', with an annex naming three commanders, at cert.cyber.gouv.fr/cti/CERTFR-2026-CTI-009/. TechTimes: the CERT-FR page 'lists no indicators of compromise' but links a full PDF. What remains open is technical proof and a court test. The other two questions are open: Reuters 'could not be independently establish[ed] whether there was any link'; no government has attributed November.
verdicts.fix: Whether France publishes technical indicators beyond its five-page attribution report or a court tests the case, and whether any government attributes the November wave. Whether the October and November waves are linked.

verdicts.evidence: New checkpoint (the whole item). Reuters does not say about a dozen. Reuters Oct. 29: malfunctions affected 'at least six' commissaries; Reuters Nov. 9: 'at least half a dozen military commissaries'. The dozen is Stars and Stripes: 'up to a dozen commissary stores were affected' per unverified sources, which the Pentagon declined to confirm. Nextgov 'about six' and 'began around late August' are right. Cyber Command is supported: Nextgov: 'Cyber Command and various Defense Department law enforcement units are probing the freezer incidents'. Also 'commissary attacks' states as fact what sources call 'suspected': Stripes: officials 'stopped short of confirming whether anything nefarious took place'.
verdicts.fix: The U.S. commissary failures, a suspected cyberattack: Reuters and Nextgov count about six, starting in late August; Stars and Stripes cites unverified reports of up to a dozen. Cyber Command is reported to be investigating.

verdicts.evidence: New checkpoint; both open on Nov. 10. No U.S. grocer report found (The Register Nov. 5; Help Net Security Nov. 9). The advisory is informational; no binding follow-up found.
Open. BleepingComputer: EFS did not name its supplier; Coolworld confirmed an incident in 'a limited number' of units; component not identified. No finding on U.S. equipment.
Open. Al Jazeera: France 'would push for European Union sanctions'; warrants 'requested'. TechTimes: 'no specific EU measures' announced.
ADT release: go-shop to Nov. 28, 2026; closing needs 'approval by ADT's stockholders and receipt of U.S. antitrust approval'.

Open. Slate deliveries 'could start as early as December' (InsideEVs); no Cyber Trust Mark product yet (Nextgov; commissioner hopes for labeled products 'within the next year', so 'late 2026' for the mark is optimistic).
Jones Day: 'Most CRA obligations apply from December 11, 2027'; Art. 13(8) support period.

Timeline event 1 (Late Aug. 2026, WATCH). Text: 'U.S. military commissary freezers are hit in a series of attacks. U.S. officials suspect Iran-linked hackers, per two anonymous sources; Reuters counts about a dozen, Nextgov about six.' Reuters counts 'at least six' (Oct. 29) and 'at least half a dozen' (Nov. 9), not a dozen. 'Are hit in a series of attacks' is stated as fact; Reuters: 'treating the malfunctions as a suspected cyberattack'; Stripes: officials 'stopped short of confirming whether anything nefarious took place'. Supported: late August; Nextgov 'about six'; 'two people familiar with the matter'.
verdicts.fix: Freezers fail at U.S. military commissaries; the Pentagon treats it as a suspected cyberattack. U.S. officials suspect Iran-linked hackers, per two anonymous sources. Reuters and Nextgov count about six stores; Stars and Stripes cites unverified reports of up to a dozen.

verdicts.evidence: Timeline event 2 (Night of Oct. 11, FACT). Reuters: 'hundreds of supermarkets'; 'as high as 50 degrees Celsius' for about six hours at Intermarche stores; fires. AP: 50 C. The Hacker News: began the night of October 11.

Timeline event 3 (Oct. 12, REPORTED). Intermarche figure is one side of a conflict. Reuters: 'around 150 of its stores'. AP: Groupement Mousquetaires said 300 Intermarche and Netto stores were impacted; The Record: 'about 300 Intermarche and Netto stores' (BFMTV); The Hacker News: 'at least 300 per AFP (about 150 per Reuters)'. Rest supported: Carrefour '80 of its supermarkets'; Monoprix '5% of its stores'; CERTFR-2026-ALE-012, Oct. 12, 'disconnect the controllers or filter access', covering AK-SM and AK-SC (SecurityWeek); PM 'instructed ... ANSSI to investigate'.
verdicts.fix: Intermarche's owner says about 150 stores were hit, per Reuters; AFP and AP put Intermarche and Netto together at about 300. Carrefour about 80, Monoprix about 5% of its stores. ...

verdicts.evidence: Timeline event 4 (Oct. 13, FACT). AP and ITV: Lescure told Parliament 'about 700 of the country's 10,000 supermarkets were affected'; prosecutor's 'cybercrime unit was investigating'. AP styles him finance minister; he holds the economy and finance portfolio.

Timeline event 5 (Oct. 13, REPORTED). Copeland/Dixell and 'declines to confirm' are right for that date (Reuters). The Cooperative U clause repeats the c020 error: the CEO said 'pas clients directs de Danfoss' and that U buys from refrigeration contractors who supply the Danfoss system.
verdicts.fix: ... Cooperative U, with 80 stores hit, says it is not a direct Danfoss customer; it buys through refrigeration contractors.

verdicts.evidence: Timeline event 6 (Oct. 26, REPORTED). Hackread, Oct. 26: 12,976 exposed service observations in 99 countries and territories, Forescout.

Timeline event 7 (Night of Nov. 1, REPORTED). IT-Connect: night of 1-2 November; sites 'notamment en Bourgogne-Franche-Comte'; contractor Coolworld; set point changed from about -30 C to 110 C. Quotidien du Medecin: on-call technician; EFS: 'aucune perte de produits sanguins n'est a declarer'; three sites. Help Net Security: investigators have not linked the blood bank incident to the supermarket attacks.

Timeline event 8 (Nov. 2, 1 a.m., FACT). The Record: Sabcobel 'began mobilising its technicians at 1 a.m.'; more than 50 stores in Belgium; 'over a dozen others' across Ireland, Estonia, the Netherlands and Luxembourg; a 'limited number' in Sweden. Help Net Security and BBC corroborate the countries. Later counts are wider (Reuters: 'more than 100 establishments'; The Record Nov. 9: at least 11 countries), which the event does not contradict but no longer reflects.

Timeline event 9 (Nov. 2, REPORTED). The Record: Rickard Nilsson: 'Heat is blowing into the freezers. Everything is ruined.'; Sabcobel about 20 units needing 'physical modifications and not just a software update'.

Timeline event 10 (Nov. 5, REPORTED). Advisory: actors may 'force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles'; authored by CISA, FBI, HHS, USDA, DoT; no U.S. victim; only 'malicious cyber actors'.

Timeline event 11 (Nov. 9, ALLEGED). NPR: ANSSI: 'around 700 different retail sites in France'; 'several small hydroelectric power plants' with 'moderate effects'; evidence as listed. The Record and TechTimes: the report names Shahid Kaveh. Prosecutor 'requesting the issuance of international arrest warrants'. Tag right.

Timeline event 12 (Nov. 10, REPORTED). Al Jazeera: 'Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said on Tuesday' (France Info) that France had summoned the ambassador and 'would push for European Union sanctions'. NPR: Iran rejected 'baseless and malicious allegations' on Tuesday. Note the summons and sanctions pledge were first announced Monday Nov. 9 (Reuters, The Record); the event reads as if they were new on the 10th.
verdicts.fix: Optional, not blocking: move the summons and sanctions to the Nov. 9 event and keep Iran's denial on Nov. 10.

verdicts.evidence: Timeline event 13 (Nov. 10, WATCH). Worded as 'no government has publicly attributed', which holds. Reuters: 'It could not be independently establish[ed] whether there was any link'. Still open today.

The id='update' paragraph. Its four tagged sentences are c001-c004: three hold, c003 does not (omits the public hacktivist claim of responsibility). Untagged parts: 'France has now named a culprit' holds; 'nothing about why the machines were exposed has changed' is the page's own judgment and is consistent with the sources (ANSSI earlier 'pointed to exposed administration and weak passwords', SentinelOne).
verdicts.fix: Replace the third sentence with: No government has attributed the November wave, the blood service attack or the U.S. commissary failures. Pro-Russian groups NoName057(16) and Z-Pentest have claimed the supermarket attacks; investigators have not confirmed those claims. U.S. officials, speaking anonymously, suspect Iran-linked hackers in the commissary cases.

verdicts.evidence: Support clock, Danfoss AK-SC 355 card (extractor misses the var D array). 'Phased out in 2016' and CERT-FR's advice both supported. Its untagged rule line, 'The EU's new rules apply only to products sold from now on', is wrong for CRA reporting (see c039).

Support clock, Danfoss AK-SM 800 card. End of life May 2021; 'hard End of Service' October 2025; more than 4,500 interfaces; 800A units on old firmware hit; CISA advisory is recommendations ('CISA recommends users take defensive measures'). Note ICSA-25-140-03 is about the AK-SM 8xxA, not the AK-SM 800 this card describes.

Support clock, Copeland E2 card, line tagged REPORTED: 'France says Copeland gear was hit in October; Copeland has not confirmed.' Present tense is no longer true. SecurityWeek, Oct. 15: Copeland 'later acknowledged a vulnerability' and is 'working with impacted customers'; Newsweek: 'Copeland confirmed a vulnerability in some discontinued controllers'. The gear CERT-FR named is Copeland XWEB and Dixell XWEB, not the E2 this card is about. Rest of card supported: E2 end of life October 2025; one critical flaw (CVE-2025-52551) affects E2; two-thirds figure; move to E3 encouraged.
verdicts.fix: Upgrade to the E3 is the maker's advice. France says Copeland XWEB and Dixell XWEB systems were hit in October; Copeland has acknowledged a vulnerability in some discontinued controllers. No E2 compromise has been reported.

verdicts.evidence: Support clock, Home router card, rule line tagged FACT: '... The U.S. Cyber Trust Mark has no products.' Same problem as c054: REPORTED at home on this page, one outlet, implied not stated. Other lines supported: FBI operation 'in more than 23 states', factory reset reverses it (DOJ); UK publication duty (gov.uk); CRA five years from Dec. 2027.
verdicts.fix: Tag the Cyber Trust Mark sentence REPORTED and add 'as of Oct. 28'.

verdicts.evidence: Support clock, Phone card. Five years after end of sale; June 20, 2025; makers promise six to seven years (heise).

Support clock, Connected car card. Slate 'doesn't include an embedded cellular modem' (Carscoops). FTC GM order, finalized Jan. 14, 2026, bars sharing certain data with consumer reporting agencies and says nothing about software support.
Support clock, Tractor card. Ten years; reset locks and immobilizers; offline mode; reports every 60 days; July 8, 2026 (DTN, FTC).

Support clock, Home security camera card. ADT agreed to be acquired by Thrive Holdings (ADT release); OpenAI holds a stake in Thrive Holdings (OpenAI); SB 327 operative Jan. 1, 2020; UK bans universal default passwords.

flags: Scope: 79 ledger claims plus 22 extras. x001-x013 are the 13 timeline events in var E; x014 is the id='update' paragraph; x015-x022 are the eight device cards in var D (the support clock), which the extractor also misses because they use chip('TAG') rather than the patterns it rewrites. That is a third blind spot beyond the two named in the task.

Ledger tags are misaligned in places: the extractor glues the previous sentence's chip text onto the next claim (e.g. c002 'ALLEGED Iran's foreign ministry ...', c003 'REPORTED The November wave ...') and for table rows swallows several cells. I judged each claim against the chip that follows it on the page, not the stray word at its start.
